items.title: Price discrimination can be welfare-enhancing
items.claim: A monopolist charges different prices to different consumer groups for the same product. Is this always bad for welfare?

options.text: Not necessarily. Price discrimination can increase output (more consumers served) and total welfare, even when redistributing surplus from consumers to firms. Whether it's welfare-positive depends on demand elasticities and whether output expands

items.reveal:
Pigou's 1920 classification: first-degree (perfect, individual reservation prices); second-degree (volume or quality discounts, e.g. Kindle Unlimited tiers); third-degree (group-based, e.g. student/senior pricing, geographic).

Schmalensee (1981) and Varian (1985) showed welfare effects depend on whether discrimination raises total output. Airlines, pharmaceuticals (Ramsey pricing across countries) and education (income-based fee remission) all use price discrimination. Personalisation through data raises new concerns about welfare and fairness.
items.why: Microeconomic textbook intuitions about welfare often need conditioning on output effects. Price discrimination is a clean example of where the textbook needs caveats.

items.title: Adam Smith warned against corporate collusion
items.claim: Adam Smith is often invoked as a free-market champion. What did he actually say about businessmen meeting together?

options.text: That free assembly among capitalists is the engine of innovation
That 'People of the same trade seldom meet together... but the conversation ends in a conspiracy against the public, or in some contrivance to raise prices.'
That competition is a myth used by economists
Nothing — he never discussed business behaviour

items.reveal:
The quote is from The Wealth of Nations (1776), Book I, Chapter X. Smith was deeply suspicious of merchant power and joint-stock companies. He criticised the East India Company at length and warned that 'the proposal of any new law or regulation of commerce which comes from this order ought always to be listened to with great precaution.'

The 'invisible hand' appears only three times in his works, with a meaning closer to 'unintended consequences of self-interested behaviour, when channelled by competition' than 'markets always good'.
items.why: Smith is invoked rhetorically by people who haven't read him. The actual Wealth of Nations is alert to monopoly, collusion and the political power of capital — closer to a regulatory liberal than a libertarian.

items.title: Switching costs create lock-in even without monopoly
items.claim: Mobile phone contracts, banking services and software subscriptions all create switching costs. How does this affect competition?

options.text: High switching costs reduce price elasticity, allow price discrimination, and create incumbency advantages; competition can shift from price-on-price to acquisition incentives that don't always benefit existing customers
Switching costs only exist in monopoly

items.reveal:
Klemperer's research (1987 onwards) formalised switching cost economics. UK's Open Banking initiative (2018), CASS (Current Account Switch Service 2013) and Ofcom's text-to-switch (2019) all aim to reduce switching frictions specifically.

The CMA's 2016 retail banking market investigation found switching costs and informational frictions sustained higher prices and weak competition.
items.why: Competition exists on a spectrum shaped by frictions. Policy can target the frictions directly (lower switching costs) rather than only firm conduct.
